questions.q: When is a design solution considered to be most appropriate?
options: When it satisfies the aesthetic requirements
When it meets the needs of the target market
When it provides strength, durability and safety
When it fulfils its intended end-use requirements
questions.explanation: Appropriateness means the design is a manageable, suitable response that effectively performs the task it was designed for — it is measured against its intended end-use. Aesthetics, durability and target market are individual factors, but appropriateness is judged against purpose and context of use.

questions.q:
A project team is conducting a needs analysis for a design project.

During the needs analysis, the team will
options: identify opportunities.
develop financial plans.
formulate a time and action plan.
establish criteria for material selection.
questions.explanation: A needs analysis is a structured exploration of the problem: it evaluates existing solutions, examines the target market and judges the potential for a future product — identifying the needs and opportunities to be met. Financial plans, time/action plans and material criteria come later, once the need is clarified.

questions.q:
A swimwear designer has been approached to develop the Australian swimsuit for the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.

What factor should be considered first?
options: Aesthetics
Durability
Function
Quality
questions.explanation: Function is the ability of a product to perform the task it was designed for. A competition swimsuit must first let an elite athlete move and swim fast — its primary function. Aesthetics matters for appeal but is secondary to how well the garment performs.

questions.q:
A design professional reviews a product that you have created and makes the comment that 'your product is really beautiful'.

To which of the following factors of design does this comment best relate?
options: Aesthetics
Ergonomics
Function
Quality
questions.explanation: Aesthetics is the physical appearance of a product and its visual appeal to the target market — form, colour, texture and proportion. A comment about beauty relates to aesthetics; ergonomics, function and quality concern fit to the user, purpose and standard of make.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes ergonomics?
options: The study of human body measurement
The design of products to satisfy a niche market
Design factors to consider in developing energy-efficient products
The study of how people work efficiently within their physical environment
questions.explanation: Ergonomics is the relationship between the human user and their physical or work environment, ensuring products are designed to fit the people who use them. The study of body measurement alone is anthropometry, which is only one of the disciplines ergonomics draws on.

questions.q: A dishwasher's main purpose is to wash and hygienically clean dinnerware, but consumers often choose between models on features such as quiet operation, energy efficiency or capacity. What is the correct term for these distinguishing extra features?
options: The product's primary function
Secondary functions, which can form the product's point of difference
The needs analysis of the product
The appropriateness of the design solution
questions.explanation: Every product has a primary function (its main purpose, the reason a consumer chooses it) and most also have secondary functions — additional features that differentiate it from competitors. That difference is called the point of difference. When you analyse function, separate the primary from the secondary functions.

questions.q: From memory: what is the 'story' used to remember the eleven factors affecting design, and which five belong to today's Part 1?
keyPoints: There are eleven factors, tagged with the marquee phrase FFA EQ NEW LOAd.

The story: a design has to do its job (function, needs, appropriateness), fit the user (aesthetics, ergonomics), be affordable and safe (finance, work health and safety), be well made (quality), and not wreck the planet (environmental consequences, obsolescence, life cycle analysis).
Today's five (Part 1) are appropriateness, needs, function, aesthetics and ergonomics — the 'does its job, fits the user' half.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the five-chunk story and named today's five factors, grade yourself Good or Easy. The story ('do its job, fit the user, be affordable and safe, be well made, don't wreck the planet') is the reliable way to hold the list — the letters alone are just a flag.

questions.q: From memory, in your own words: how do designers use anthropometric data to size a product such as a chair or a door handle?
keyPoints: Anthropometry is the study of human body sizes and shapes — tables of body measurements across a population.
Because humans vary in size, you can't design for one person; the standard principle is to design for the range from roughly the 5th to the 95th percentile.
The 5th percentile is a small user (only 5% are smaller) and the 95th is a large user (only 5% are larger), so designing to that range accommodates about 90% of users.
Seat height, handle reach and doorway width are set from anthropometric tables, not guessed.
questions.explanation: If you stated the 5th-to-95th-percentile reasoning and linked it to fitting real measured human bodies, grade yourself Good or Easy. 'It's about comfort' is a band-four answer; the data-driven percentile version is what scores in the exam.

questions.q: Why do designers consider ergonomic factors when designing a new product?
questions.modelAnswer: Ergonomics is the relationship between the human user and their physical or work environment, ensuring a product is designed to fit the people intended to use it, using data such as anthropometry. Designers consider it because a well-designed, ergonomic product is comfortable, safe and productive, whereas failing to consider ergonomics can cause the user discomfort, pain or physical injury.

criteria.descriptor: Sketches in general terms ergonomic factors that may be considered by a designer when developing a new product

questions.explanation: The trap is defining ergonomics as just 'comfort'. It is the measured fit between the user and the design — name that fit, link it to comfort/safety/productivity, and contrast it with the discomfort, pain or injury caused by ignoring it.

questions.q: What role does aesthetics play in influencing consumer purchasing decisions?
questions.modelAnswer: Aesthetics is the physical appearance of a product and its visual appeal to the target market — its form, colour, texture and proportion. It strongly influences purchasing decisions because a product with poor aesthetics may not attract users even if it functions well, while strong visual appeal draws consumers and can be the deciding factor when products perform similarly. For products where appearance matters most, such as a perfume bottle, aesthetics carries enormous weight; for others, such as a surgeon's scalpel, function dominates. Successful designs therefore balance function and aesthetics for their specific target market, and it is often the aesthetic appeal that converts interest into a purchase.

criteria.descriptor: Makes the relationship evident between aesthetic factors and consumer purchasing decisions, through cause and effect statements
Provides characteristics and features of the relationship between aesthetic factors and consumer purchasing decisions, using examples
Identifies an aesthetic factor OR consumer purchasing decisions

questions.explanation: To reach the top band, link aesthetics to purchasing through cause and effect, not assertion: poor aesthetics deters buyers, strong appeal attracts them, and how much it matters depends on the product and target market.
